summary: Botopasi Airport (BTO) is a small airstrip serving the remote Trio (Tiriyó) indigenous village of Botopasi in the Sipaliwini District of southern Suriname, deep within the Amazon rainforest. The airport functions as a critical lifeline for the isolated community, supporting passenger transport, mail delivery, and medical evacuation flights. It is primarily used by small charter and bush planes operated by local carriers connecting remote interior villages to Paramaribo.
faqs:
Q: What airlines serve Botopasi Airport?
A: Small charter and bush plane operators such as Gum Air and Blue Wing Airlines historically serve Botopasi, though scheduled service is limited and subject to weather and demand.

Q: How long is the runway at Botopasi Airport?
A: The airport features a short unpaved gravel/dirt runway suitable only for small STOL (Short Takeoff and Landing) aircraft.

Q: Are there facilities at Botopasi Airport?
A: No terminal building or commercial services are available; the airstrip is basic with minimal infrastructure typical of remote Surinamese interior airfields.

Q: When is the best time to fly to Botopasi?
A: The dry season (roughly August to November) generally offers the most reliable flying conditions, as heavy rainfall can cause delays or cancellations during the wet season.
transport_tips: There is no road access to Botopasi; the only practical way to reach the village is by small aircraft. Passengers typically arrange flights through charter operators in Paramaribo, often as part of multi-stop interior routes. Upon landing, the village is a short walk from the airstrip, and local transport is arranged on foot or by small boat along the Tapanahony River.
local_tip: Bring all essential supplies, including food, water, insect repellent, and cash, as Botopasi has no shops or ATMs—everything must be brought in or sourced from the village's small trading posts. Communication is also limited, so inform someone in Paramaribo of your travel plans in advance.
